main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Explain the basic concepts of Biology (meaning, branches, basic terminologies, importance and its relationship with other disciplines)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students accurately define biology and correctly categorise at least three branches of biology with examples.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts showing branches of Biology|Textbooks|Manila paper for group work|Online resources
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Biology is the natural science that studies living organisms, including their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution and distribution. It helps us understand how life exists and works.
sla_notes_details: The major branches of biology include botany (study of plants), zoology (study of animals), microbiology (study of microorganisms), ecology (study of interactions between organisms and their environment) and genetics (study of heredity). Basic terminologies used in biology include organism, cell, tissue, organ, species and habitat. Biology is closely related to other disciplines such as chemistry, physics, geography and mathematics, which provide tools and knowledge for biological investigations.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a botanist studying how a bean plant grows uses botany, while a doctor treating malaria applies knowledge from microbiology and human physiology to understand the disease and its treatment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of biology helps people make informed decisions about health, nutrition, farming and conservation of the environment in their daily lives.
sla_exercise: What is biology?::Biology is the science that studies living organisms and their life processes.||Name two branches of biology.::Botany (study of plants) and zoology (study of animals).||Why is biology important to human life?::It helps in understanding health, disease prevention, food production and conservation of the environment.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe a cell (meaning, types, structures and functions)
sla_name: The Cell as the Basic Unit of Life
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify the meaning of a cell and distinguish between plant and animal cell structures and their functions.
sla_teaching_aids: Light microscope|Prepared slides|Cell charts/models|Onion and cheek cell specimens
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of a living organism, capable of carrying out all life processes. All living things are made up of one or more cells.
sla_notes_details: There are two main types of cells: prokaryotic cells, which lack a true nucleus (found in bacteria), and eukaryotic cells, which have a true nucleus (found in plants, animals, fungi and protists). Plant cells have a cell wall, large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts, while animal cells lack these structures but have small temporary vacuoles. Common structures found in most cells include the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria, each performing specific functions such as control of cell activities, energy production and protection of the cell.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when an onion epidermis cell is viewed under a light microscope, one can clearly see the rectangular cell wall, nucleus and cytoplasm, while a human cheek cell viewed under the same microscope shows an irregular shape without a cell wall.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding cell structure helps us appreciate how our bodies grow, repair wounds and fight diseases at the cellular level.
sla_exercise: Define a cell.::A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of a living organism.||State one structural difference between a plant cell and an animal cell.::A plant cell has a cell wall and chloroplasts while an animal cell does not.||What is the function of the nucleus in a cell?::The nucleus controls all the activities of the cell and contains genetic material (DNA).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe nutrition in plants (photosynthesis, leaf structure and mineral requirements)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the process of photosynthesis, the structure of a leaf and the mineral requirements necessary for healthy plant growth.
sla_teaching_aids: Fresh leaves|Charts of leaf structure|Potted plants|Water and mineral nutrient samples
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutrition in plants mainly occurs through photosynthesis, the process by which green plants manufacture their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
sla_notes_details: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves, which are structurally adapted for this process through features such as a broad flat lamina, thin cuticle, numerous stomata for gas exchange and chlorophyll-containing chloroplasts in the mesophyll cells. The overall word equation for photosynthesis is carbon dioxide plus water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, producing glucose and oxygen. Apart from photosynthesis, plants also require essential mineral elements such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which are absorbed from the soil through roots to support growth, root development and overall health.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a leaf tested for starch after exposure to sunlight turns blue-black with iodine solution, showing that photosynthesis has taken place, while a leaf kept in the dark shows no colour change.
sla_notes_daily_life: Photosynthesis is the foundation of most food chains, providing food for humans and animals, and mineral fertilizers are applied by farmers to boost crop yields.
sla_exercise: Write the raw materials needed for photosynthesis.::Carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.||Name one structural adaptation of a leaf for photosynthesis.::Presence of stomata for gas exchange (or a broad lamina for light absorption).||State one mineral element required by plants and its importance.::Nitrogen is required for the formation of proteins and healthy leaf growth.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of scientific biological terminologies
learning_activity_name: Explain the concept and systems of classification (meaning ,importance of classification, rules of scientific naming of organisms, artificial and natural classification systems)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain the meaning and importance of classification and apply the binomial rules of scientific naming.
sla_teaching_aids: Classification charts|Variety of living organism specimens|Textbooks|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Classification is the systematic arrangement of living organisms into groups based on their similarities and differences in structure and function.
sla_notes_details: Classification is important because it makes the study of the many different living organisms easier, shows evolutionary relationships and helps to identify and name new organisms. Organisms are scientifically named using the binomial nomenclature system, which gives each organism a two-part Latin name consisting of the genus and species, for example Homo sapiens for humans. There are two systems of classification: artificial classification, which groups organisms based on a few convenient visible characteristics, and natural classification, which groups organisms based on many shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the scientific name of a domestic cat is Felis catus, where 'Felis' is the genus and 'catus' is the species, following the binomial naming rule of capitalizing the genus and writing the species in lowercase, both italicised.
sla_notes_daily_life: Classification helps doctors, farmers and conservationists to correctly identify harmful and useful organisms, such as distinguishing edible mushrooms from poisonous ones.
sla_exercise: What is classification?::Classification is the systematic grouping of living organisms based on their similarities and differences.||State one rule of the binomial system of naming organisms.::The genus name is written first with a capital letter and the species name follows in lowercase, both italicised or underlined.||Give one importance of classifying living organisms.::It makes the study of organisms easier and helps show relationships between different organisms.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of scientific biological terminologies
learning_activity_name: Describe the major groups of organisms: (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia and Viruses)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify and describe the characteristics of each of the five kingdoms and viruses.
sla_teaching_aids: Preserved specimens|Classification charts|Microscope|Pictures of representative organisms
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Living organisms are broadly grouped into five kingdoms, namely Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, based on their cell structure, mode of nutrition and body organisation, while viruses form a separate, non-cellular group.
sla_notes_details: Kingdom Monera consists of unicellular prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria; Protista consists of simple eukaryotic organisms such as Amoeba and algae; Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that feed by absorbing nutrients, such as mushrooms and moulds; Plantae are multicellular organisms that make their own food through photosynthesis; and Animalia are multicellular organisms that feed on other organisms. Viruses are microscopic, non-cellular particles that can only reproduce inside a living host cell and are therefore considered to be at the border between living and non-living things.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Escherichia coli represents kingdom Monera, Amoeba represents Protista, mushroom represents Fungi, maize plant represents Plantae, and a dog represents Animalia, while the influenza virus is an example of a virus.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of these groups helps in understanding diseases caused by bacteria and viruses, and in using fungi such as yeast in baking and brewing.
sla_exercise: Name the five kingdoms of living organisms.::Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.||Why are viruses not classified in any of the five kingdoms?::Because they are non-cellular and can only reproduce inside a living host cell, unlike organisms in the five kingdoms.||Give one example of an organism in kingdom Fungi.::Mushroom (or yeast/mould).

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic skills for conducting biological experiments (observation, measurement and experimentation)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify common laboratory apparatus and describe the basic skills of observation, measurement and experimentation.
sla_teaching_aids: Rulers|Weighing scales|Thermometers|Beakers and other laboratory apparatus
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Conducting biological investigations requires basic scientific skills, namely observation, measurement and experimentation, which allow learners to gather accurate and reliable information about living organisms.
sla_notes_details: Observation involves using the senses, sometimes aided by instruments such as a hand lens or microscope, to gather information about an organism or process. Measurement involves the use of appropriate instruments such as rulers, weighing scales and thermometers to obtain quantitative data such as length, mass and temperature. Experimentation involves designing and carrying out a controlled test to investigate a biological question, ensuring that only one variable is changed at a time while others are kept constant.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when investigating the effect of light on plant growth, a student uses a ruler to measure the height of the plant every day (measurement), records the colour and appearance of the leaves (observation), and sets up two plants, one in light and one in darkness, to compare growth (experimentation).
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills are used by farmers to monitor crop growth, and by health workers to measure a patient's temperature and weight during check-ups.
sla_exercise: Name the three basic skills required for conducting a biological investigation.::Observation, measurement and experimentation.||Which instrument is used to measure the mass of a specimen?::A weighing scale (or balance).||What is a controlled experiment?::An experiment in which only one variable is changed while all other conditions are kept constant.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Carry out microscopic observation of a cell
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly prepare a microscope slide and identify visible cell structures under the light microscope.
sla_teaching_aids: Light microscope|Microscope slides and cover slips|Onion bulb|Iodine solution
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Microscopic observation of a cell involves the use of a light microscope to view and study the structure of cells that are too small to be seen with the naked eye.
sla_notes_details: To observe a cell, a thin section of tissue, such as the inner epidermis of an onion, is placed on a microscope slide, stained with a suitable stain such as iodine solution to make structures more visible, and covered with a cover slip before being viewed under low and then high magnification. Under the microscope, structures such as the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus can be identified and their arrangement observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a stained onion epidermal cell is viewed under the microscope at low power, rectangular cells with a visible cell wall and a darkly stained nucleus can be clearly seen and drawn.
sla_notes_daily_life: Microscopic techniques are used in hospitals and laboratories to diagnose diseases by examining blood and tissue samples.
sla_exercise: Which instrument is used to observe cells that are too small to see with the naked eye?::A light microscope.||Why is iodine solution used when preparing an onion cell slide?::It stains the cell structures, such as the nucleus, making them more visible under the microscope.||Name two cell structures that can be seen when observing a stained onion cell under a microscope.::The cell wall and the nucleus.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Carry out investigations related to photosynthesis (conditions necessary for photosynthesis)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly design and carry out an experiment to test the necessity of light, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
sla_teaching_aids: Potted plants|Variegated leaves|Iodine solution|Beakers, ethanol and source of heat
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigations on photosynthesis are carried out to prove that factors such as light, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide are necessary for the process to occur.
sla_notes_details: A common investigation involves destarching a potted plant by keeping it in darkness for 48 hours, then exposing part of a leaf to light while covering another part with black paper, and testing both parts for starch using the iodine test after boiling the leaf in water and then ethanol to remove chlorophyll. A blue-black colour with iodine indicates the presence of starch, showing that photosynthesis has occurred, while a leaf part that remains brown shows no photosynthesis took place.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a variegated leaf with green and white patches is tested for starch, only the green chlorophyll-containing parts turn blue-black, proving that chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers use knowledge from such investigations to ensure crops receive adequate sunlight for maximum food production and yield.
sla_exercise: Why is a potted plant destarched before an investigation on photosynthesis?::To remove any existing starch so that any starch found afterwards results from the investigation, not from before.||What colour change indicates the presence of starch in the iodine test?::The leaf turns blue-black in the presence of starch.||Name one factor necessary for photosynthesis that can be tested using a variegated leaf.::Chlorophyll.

specific_competence_name: Prepare and present results of biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Prepare and present a report on cell and photosynthesis investigations
sla_name: Writing a Report on Cell and Photosynthesis Investigations
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly prepare and present a scientific report following the standard steps of report writing.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample investigation report format|Manila paper|Markers|Students' recorded data
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A scientific investigation report is a written record that communicates the aim, procedure, results and conclusion of a biological investigation in a clear and logical manner.
sla_notes_details: A good biological investigation report includes the title, aim/objective, materials and apparatus used, procedure followed, observations or results, often presented in tables or diagrams, discussion of results, and a conclusion that answers the original question. When reporting on cell and photosynthesis investigations, students should include labelled diagrams of the cells observed and clearly state whether starch was present or absent in the photosynthesis test.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a report on the photosynthesis investigation would present a table comparing the leaf parts covered and uncovered with black paper and the resulting iodine test colour for each, followed by a conclusion that light is necessary for photosynthesis.
sla_notes_daily_life: Report writing skills learned here are useful in many careers, such as in agriculture and health, where accurate record keeping and communication of findings is essential.
sla_exercise: List two parts that should be included in a biological investigation report.::Title/aim and procedure (also materials, results and conclusion).||Why should a report include a conclusion?::The conclusion states whether the results support the aim of the investigation, answering the original question.||What should be included when reporting the results of a cell observation investigation?::A clearly labelled diagram of the cell structures observed under the microscope.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe nutrition in human and ruminants (nutrients, digestive system and processes)
sla_name: Nutrition and Digestion in Humans and Ruminants
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the classes of food nutrients and explain the digestive processes in humans and ruminants.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of human digestive system|Charts of ruminant digestive system|Food samples|Dissected mammal specimen
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food for energy, growth and repair. In humans and ruminants, food is broken down through digestion before it can be absorbed and used by the body.
sla_notes_details: The main classes of food nutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and fibre, each with specific functions in the body. In humans, digestion occurs in the alimentary canal, starting from the mouth, where food is chewed and mixed with saliva, through the stomach and small intestine, where enzymes break down nutrients into simpler absorbable forms. Ruminants, such as cattle, have a specialised four-chambered stomach, the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum, that allows them to digest cellulose from plant material through microbial fermentation and rumination (chewing the cud).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a cow swallows grass with little chewing, later regurgitates it as cud to chew again, illustrating how the rumen allows microbes to break down tough plant fibre that humans cannot digest.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding balanced nutrition helps people plan healthy diets, while knowledge of ruminant digestion helps farmers feed cattle appropriately for better milk and meat production.
sla_exercise: Name three classes of food nutrients.::Carbohydrates, proteins and fats (also vitamins, minerals, water and fibre).||What is rumination in ruminants?::The process of regurgitating swallowed food (cud) back to the mouth for further chewing.||Which organ in ruminants digests cellulose through microbial action?::The rumen.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanism of transportation of materials in flowering plants (vascular system, absorption and movement of water and mineral salts and transpiration)
sla_name: Transport of Materials in Flowering Plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the vascular system of plants and explain how water, mineral salts and transpiration occur.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of plant vascular tissue|Celery stalk stained with dye|Potted plants|Hand lens
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Flowering plants transport water, mineral salts and manufactured food through a specialised vascular system made up of xylem and phloem tissues.
sla_notes_details: Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to other parts of the plant, while phloem tissue transports manufactured food, mainly sucrose, from the leaves to other parts of the plant, a process called translocation. Water and mineral salts are absorbed by root hairs through osmosis and active transport, and move upward through the xylem due to root pressure, capillary action and transpiration pull. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the plant, mainly through stomata on the leaves, which helps to draw water upward and cool the plant.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a white flower stem is placed in water containing red dye, the dye can be seen travelling up the stem through the xylem vessels, colouring the veins of the petals red.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers apply fertilizers to the soil so that mineral salts can be absorbed by roots and transported to all parts of the crop for healthy growth.
sla_exercise: Name the two types of vascular tissue in plants and their functions.::Xylem transports water and mineral salts; phloem transports manufactured food.||What is transpiration?::The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves.||Through which plant structures do water and mineral salts enter the roots?::Through root hairs.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanism of transportation of materials in the human body (the mammalian heart, blood vessels, blood, blood circulation)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the structure of the heart, blood vessels and blood, and explain the circulation of blood in the body.
sla_teaching_aids: Heart model/charts|Charts of blood vessels|Microscope slides of blood cells|Stethoscope
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The human circulatory system transports materials such as oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste products around the body through blood, pumped by the heart and carried in blood vessels.
sla_notes_details: The mammalian heart is a muscular, four-chambered pump consisting of two atria and two ventricles that pump deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. Blood is carried in three main types of vessels: arteries, which carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; veins, which carry blood back to the heart; and capillaries, which allow exchange of substances between blood and body tissues. Blood itself is composed of plasma, red blood cells, which carry oxygen using haemoglobin, white blood cells, which fight infection, and platelets, which help in clotting.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle of the heart through the aorta, travels through arteries to body tissues where oxygen is exchanged for carbon dioxide in capillaries, and returns as deoxygenated blood through veins to the right atrium of the heart.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding blood circulation helps in recognising the importance of exercise for heart health and in understanding conditions such as high blood pressure.
sla_exercise: Name the four chambers of the mammalian heart.::Two atria (left and right) and two ventricles (left and right).||Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?::Arteries.||What is the function of red blood cells?::They carry oxygen around the body using haemoglobin.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanisms of gaseous exchange and respiration in mammals (gaseous exchange in mammals, aerobic and anaerobic respiration)
sla_name: Gaseous Exchange and Respiration in Mammals
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the process of gaseous exchange in the lungs and distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of lungs and alveoli|Model of respiratory system|Balloons for lung capacity demonstration
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Gaseous exchange in mammals occurs in the lungs, where oxygen from inhaled air diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be exhaled, while respiration is the process of releasing energy from food inside cells.
sla_notes_details: The lungs contain millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, which are surrounded by capillaries and provide a large, thin, moist surface area for efficient diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Respiration can be aerobic, which uses oxygen to completely break down glucose into carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy, or anaerobic, which occurs without oxygen and releases less energy, producing lactic acid in muscle cells or ethanol and carbon dioxide in some microorganisms.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, during vigorous exercise when oxygen supply to muscles is insufficient, muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid, which causes muscle fatigue and cramps.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding respiration explains why athletes breathe heavily after intense exercise and why regular physical activity improves lung and heart efficiency.
sla_exercise: Where does gaseous exchange occur in mammals?::In the alveoli of the lungs.||State one difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.::Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases more energy, while anaerobic respiration does not use oxygen and releases less energy.||What substance is produced in human muscles during anaerobic respiration?::Lactic acid.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanism of gaseous exchange in plants (parts of plants responsible for gaseous exchange and the process)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify plant structures responsible for gaseous exchange and describe how the process occurs.
sla_teaching_aids: Leaf specimens|Charts showing stomata structure|Hand lens|Microscope
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Gaseous exchange in plants is the process by which plants take in and release gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide with the surrounding environment, mainly through the leaves and stems.
sla_notes_details: In leaves, gaseous exchange mainly occurs through tiny pores called stomata, found mostly on the lower surface of the leaf, which open and close through the action of guard cells to regulate gas and water movement. Woody stems exchange gases through small openings called lenticels, while roots exchange gases with air spaces in the soil. During the day, plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and release oxygen, while at night, without sunlight, they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide through respiration.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when the underside of a leaf is examined under a microscope, numerous small stomata bordered by kidney-shaped guard cells can be observed, showing how gases move in and out of the leaf.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding gaseous exchange in plants explains why it is beneficial to keep plants in living spaces during the day, as they absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
sla_exercise: Name the structure through which most gaseous exchange occurs in a leaf.::Stomata.||What is the function of guard cells?::They control the opening and closing of stomata.||Through which structures do woody stems exchange gases?::Lenticels.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate food nutrients in various food samples
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly carry out food tests and accurately identify the nutrients present in given food samples.
sla_teaching_aids: Iodine solution|Benedict's solution|Biuret solution|Ethanol|Food samples and test tubes
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Food tests are scientific procedures used to identify which nutrients, such as starch, reducing sugar, protein and fat, are present in a given food sample.
sla_notes_details: The iodine test detects starch, turning blue-black when starch is present; Benedict's test detects reducing sugars, forming a brick-red precipitate when heated with a sugar-containing sample; the Biuret test detects proteins, turning the sample purple/violet in the presence of protein; and the ethanol emulsion test detects fats, forming a white milky emulsion when a fat sample is mixed with ethanol and then water.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, testing a sample of cooked rice with iodine solution produces a blue-black colour, confirming the presence of starch, while testing a groundnut sample with the ethanol emulsion test produces a white cloudy emulsion, confirming the presence of fat.
sla_notes_daily_life: Food tests help people and food scientists check the nutritional content of foods to ensure a balanced diet and detect adulteration.
sla_exercise: Which reagent is used to test for starch and what colour change indicates a positive result?::Iodine solution; it turns blue-black in the presence of starch.||What colour change indicates a positive Biuret test for protein?::The solution turns purple/violet.||Name the test used to detect fats in a food sample.::The ethanol emulsion test.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate processes of transportation of materials in flowering plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly set up and interpret an experiment demonstrating the pathway of water transport in a flowering plant.
sla_teaching_aids: White flowers/celery stalks|Red or blue dye|Beakers|Razor blade|Hand lens
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigations on transportation of materials in flowering plants demonstrate how water moves from the roots or stem upward through the xylem to the leaves and flowers.
sla_notes_details: A common investigation involves placing the cut stem of a white flower or a celery stalk into water coloured with dye and leaving it for some hours. After the set time, the stem is cut transversely and longitudinally to observe the coloured vascular bundles, showing the pathway followed by the water and dye. This demonstrates that water moves upward through xylem vessels located in the vascular bundles of the stem.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after several hours in blue dye, a white carnation flower shows blue-coloured veins in its petals, and a cross-section of its stem shows coloured dots corresponding to the xylem vessels.
sla_notes_daily_life: This investigation helps explain how cut flowers absorb water to stay fresh, and how farmers can apply water-soluble fertilizers that are absorbed and transported through the plant.
sla_exercise: Why is dye added to water in this investigation?::To make the pathway of water movement through the plant visible.||Which plant tissue is responsible for transporting the coloured water upward?::Xylem tissue.||How can the pathway of water transport be observed in the stem?::By cutting the stem transversely or longitudinally and observing the coloured vascular bundles.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Carry out experiments to determine the pulse rate in human
sla_assessment_criteria: Students accurately measure and record pulse rate at rest and after exercise, and explain the observed differences.
sla_teaching_aids: Stopwatch|Blood pressure machine|Recording sheets
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Pulse rate is the number of times an artery expands and contracts per minute as blood is pumped through it by the heart, and it can be used to estimate heart rate.
sla_notes_details: Pulse rate is commonly measured at the wrist (radial artery) or neck (carotid artery) by placing two fingers gently on the artery and counting the beats felt for a set time, usually 15 or 30 seconds, then multiplying to get beats per minute. A normal resting pulse rate for a healthy young person is typically between 60 and 100 beats per minute, and it increases during and after physical exercise because the body needs more oxygen and nutrients delivered to the muscles.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student may record a resting pulse rate of 72 beats per minute, but after running for two minutes, the pulse rate rises to about 120 beats per minute, showing the effect of exercise on heart activity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Measuring pulse rate is a simple health check used by nurses and fitness trainers to monitor a person's heart function and fitness level.
sla_exercise: Where on the body can a pulse commonly be measured?::At the wrist (radial artery) or the neck (carotid artery).||What happens to pulse rate immediately after exercise?::It increases, because the heart beats faster to supply more oxygen to the muscles.||State the normal resting pulse rate range for a healthy young person.::About 60 to 100 beats per minute.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly set up experiments demonstrating aerobic and anaerobic respiration and interpret the results.
sla_teaching_aids: Germinating seeds|Yeast and sugar solution|Limewater|Test tubes and delivery tubes
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigations on respiration are carried out to demonstrate that living organisms release carbon dioxide and energy during aerobic respiration, and that some organisms can respire anaerobically without oxygen.
sla_notes_details: In an aerobic respiration investigation, germinating seeds are placed in a flask connected to limewater; the limewater turns milky due to carbon dioxide produced by respiration. In an anaerobic respiration investigation, yeast is mixed with a sugar solution in a test tube with a delivery tube leading to limewater, and the mixture is kept without oxygen, for example covered with oil; bubbling and cloudiness in the limewater and a smell of alcohol indicate anaerobic respiration (fermentation) is taking place.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after setting up germinating seeds connected to limewater for a day, the limewater turns milky, confirming that carbon dioxide is released, while a yeast and sugar mixture kept anaerobically produces bubbles of carbon dioxide and a faint smell of ethanol.
sla_notes_daily_life: Anaerobic respiration by yeast is used in baking to make bread rise and in brewing to produce alcoholic drinks.
sla_exercise: What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide is passed through it?::It turns milky/cloudy.||What gas is produced by yeast during anaerobic respiration (fermentation)?::Carbon dioxide.||Why is oil sometimes added on top of a yeast and sugar mixture during this investigation?::To prevent oxygen from entering, ensuring the yeast respires anaerobically.

specific_competence_name: Prepare and present results of biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Prepare and present a report of a biological investigation on ( food nutrients in various food samples, transportation of materials in flowering plants, pulse rate in human, aerobic and anaerobic respiration )
sla_name: Reporting Investigations on Nutrition, Transport and Respiration
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly prepare and present a scientific report of one of the term's investigations using the standard scientific procedure.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample report format|Students' data and observations|Manila paper and markers
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Preparing and presenting an investigation report allows students to systematically communicate the procedures and findings of their biological investigations to others.
sla_notes_details: A report on these investigations should follow the standard scientific format, including the aim of the investigation, materials and apparatus used, step-by-step procedure, results, in tables where the food tests, dye colour observed, pulse rate readings or gas bubble counts are recorded, and a conclusion linking the results to the aim. When presenting, students should clearly explain their findings, such as which nutrients were present in a food sample, how water moved through a plant, how pulse rate changed with exercise, or the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group presenting on the pulse rate investigation would show a bar graph comparing resting and post-exercise pulse rates and explain that exercise increases the pulse rate due to increased oxygen demand by muscles.
sla_notes_daily_life: These reporting skills are essential in scientific, health and agricultural careers where findings must be recorded and communicated accurately to others.
sla_exercise: What should the results section of an investigation report contain?::The data and observations collected during the investigation, often presented in tables or graphs.||Why is it important to state a clear aim in an investigation report?::It guides the reader on what the investigation intended to find out and helps in drawing a relevant conclusion.||Name one investigation from this term that could be included in the report.::Investigation of food nutrients in food samples (or pulse rate, transport in plants, or aerobic/anaerobic respiration).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe coordination in plants (tropic responses) and animals (nervous coordination in human, structure of neurones, sense organs and endocrine system)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe tropic responses in plants and explain nervous and hormonal coordination in humans, including neurone structure and sense organs.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of neurone structure|Models of sense organs|Potted plants for tropism demonstration|Charts of endocrine glands
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Coordination is the way organisms respond and adjust to changes in their environment. In plants this occurs through tropic responses, while in animals it occurs through the nervous system and endocrine (hormonal) system.
sla_notes_details: Tropic responses are growth movements of plants in response to stimuli such as light (phototropism), gravity (geotropism) and water (hydrotropism). In humans, nervous coordination involves the brain, spinal cord and nerves, made up of specialised cells called neurones that transmit electrical impulses; a typical neurone has a cell body, dendrites and a long axon. Sense organs, such as the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin, detect stimuli from the environment and send signals to the brain, while the endocrine system consists of glands, such as the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands, that release hormones directly into the blood to regulate body processes more slowly than nerves.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a plant shoot placed near a window bends and grows towards the light due to positive phototropism, while when a person touches a hot object, sensory receptors in the skin send an impulse through nerves to the spinal cord, triggering a rapid reflex withdrawal of the hand.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding coordination explains why plants in a room grow towards a window, and how the human body reacts quickly to danger through reflexes to prevent injury.
sla_exercise: What is phototropism?::The growth response of a plant towards or away from light.||Name the basic functional unit of the nervous system.::A neurone (nerve cell).||Give one example of an endocrine gland and one hormone it produces.::The pancreas produces insulin (or the thyroid produces thyroxine).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanism of excretion in the human body (systems: organs, products)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify the organs of excretion and describe the excretory products removed from the human body.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of the human urinary system|Kidney model|Charts of skin structure
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products from the body, which, if allowed to accumulate, would be harmful to the organism.
sla_notes_details: The main excretory organs in humans include the kidneys, which filter blood to remove urea, excess water and salts, forming urine; the lungs, which remove carbon dioxide and water vapour during breathing; the skin, which removes excess water, salts and a small amount of urea through sweat; and the liver, which breaks down toxic substances such as excess amino acids into urea. Each kidney is made up of thousands of tiny filtering units called nephrons, which filter blood under pressure and then selectively reabsorb useful substances back into the blood before urine is formed and passed to the bladder through the ureters.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, on a hot day, the body loses more water and salts through sweating from the skin, while the kidneys compensate by producing more concentrated, darker urine to conserve water in the body.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding excretion helps explain why drinking enough water is important for kidney health, and why doctors may test urine to check for kidney disorders such as diabetes.
sla_exercise: Name the main organ responsible for filtering blood and forming urine.::The kidney.||What is the main nitrogenous waste product removed by the kidneys?::Urea.||Name two excretory organs apart from the kidneys.::The lungs and the skin (also the liver).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanism of regulation in the human body (temperature regulation, blood sugar regulation and osmoregulation)
sla_name: Homeostasis: Regulation in the Human Body
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain how the human body regulates temperature, blood sugar level and water/salt balance.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts on skin structure and thermoregulation|Charts on blood sugar regulation|Charts on the kidney and osmoregulation
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Regulation, also called homeostasis, is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body despite changes in the external environment, and includes control of body temperature, blood sugar level and water/salt balance.
sla_notes_details: Temperature regulation is controlled mainly by the skin and the hypothalamus in the brain; when the body is hot, sweating and dilation of skin blood vessels increase heat loss, while when the body is cold, shivering and constriction of skin blood vessels reduce heat loss. Blood sugar regulation is controlled by the pancreas through the hormones insulin, which lowers blood glucose by promoting its uptake and storage as glycogen, and glucagon, which raises blood glucose by converting stored glycogen back to glucose. Osmoregulation is the control of water and salt balance in the body, mainly carried out by the kidneys under the influence of the hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone), which regulates the amount of water reabsorbed and therefore the concentration of urine produced.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after eating a sugary meal, blood glucose level rises, stimulating the pancreas to release insulin, which lowers the blood glucose back to normal by promoting its storage in the liver as glycogen.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding blood sugar regulation helps explain diabetes, a condition where the body fails to properly regulate blood sugar, and understanding temperature regulation explains why people sweat more in hot weather.
sla_exercise: Which hormone lowers blood glucose level, and which organ produces it?::Insulin, produced by the pancreas.||Name one way the body loses heat when it is too hot.::Sweating (or dilation of skin blood vessels).||Which hormone regulates water reabsorption in the kidney?::Antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate the process of nervous coordination (reflex arc and knee jerk)
sla_name: Investigating the Reflex Arc and Knee Jerk
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly demonstrate the knee jerk reflex and explain the pathway of a reflex arc.
sla_teaching_aids: Reflex hammer (or improvised rubber mallet)|Charts of the reflex arc|Chair for the demonstration
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A reflex action is an automatic, rapid and involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought, and it follows a specific pathway called a reflex arc.
sla_notes_details: A reflex arc consists of a receptor that detects the stimulus, a sensory neurone that carries the impulse to the spinal cord, a relay (connector) neurone in the spinal cord, a motor neurone that carries the impulse to an effector, and the effector, usually a muscle, that carries out the response. The knee jerk reflex is investigated by having a person sit with legs crossed and tapping just below the kneecap with a light hammer; this stretches a tendon, stimulating a receptor that sends an impulse through a reflex arc, causing the leg to kick forward involuntarily.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when the patellar tendon below the knee is tapped, the leg immediately jerks forward without the person consciously deciding to move it, demonstrating a spinal reflex that bypasses the brain.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reflexes such as blinking when an object approaches the eye or withdrawing a hand from a hot surface protect the body from harm by producing very fast responses.
sla_exercise: What is a reflex action?::An automatic, rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus.||List the five components of a reflex arc in order.::Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.||Which tendon is tapped to produce the knee jerk reflex?::The patellar tendon (below the kneecap).

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate tropic responses in plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly design and carry out an experiment to demonstrate a tropic response in plants and record their observations.
sla_teaching_aids: Seedlings|Pots and soil|Boxes to exclude light|Water
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigating tropic responses helps learners to demonstrate, through experiments, how plants respond by growth movements to stimuli such as light and gravity.
sla_notes_details: To investigate phototropism, seedlings are grown in a box with a small hole allowing light from only one direction; after some days, the shoots are observed to bend and grow towards the hole, showing positive phototropism. To investigate geotropism, a pot of germinating seeds can be placed on its side; after some days, the roots are observed to grow downward (positive geotropism) while the shoots grow upward (negative geotropism), regardless of the pot's orientation.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a germinating bean seed is placed sideways in soil, within a few days the root curves and grows downward while the shoot curves and grows upward, demonstrating that roots and shoots respond oppositely to gravity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding tropic responses helps farmers and gardeners position seedlings correctly and understand why plants near a window always bend and grow towards the light.
sla_exercise: What is positive phototropism?::Growth of a plant part, such as a shoot, towards a source of light.||How do roots typically respond to gravity?::Roots grow downward, showing positive geotropism.||Name one apparatus needed to investigate phototropism in seedlings.::A box with a single hole to allow light from one direction.

specific_competence_name: Carry out a biological project work using biological principles
learning_activity_name: Develop and carry out a simple research project in Biology
sla_name: Developing a Simple Biology Research Project
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly develop a research question, plan and begin carrying out a simple biology research project using appropriate scientific procedures.
sla_teaching_aids: Reference textbooks|Notebooks for project planning|Materials relevant to the chosen project topic
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A biology research project is an extended, guided investigation in which students select a biological problem, plan a method to study it, and carry out the investigation systematically over a period of time.
sla_notes_details: Developing a research project involves several steps: selecting a suitable and researchable topic, stating a clear aim and hypothesis, identifying the materials and procedure needed, and planning how data will be collected and recorded. Students then begin carrying out the project following their plan, making regular observations and keeping accurate records, while ensuring that the investigation follows sound scientific principles such as fair testing and appropriate use of controls.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group of students may choose the topic 'Effect of different types of manure on the growth of maize seedlings', plan to grow three sets of seedlings under different manure treatments, and begin recording the height of the seedlings weekly.
sla_notes_daily_life: Research skills developed through such projects are valuable in agriculture, health and environmental work, where identifying and solving real-life problems scientifically is important.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in developing a research project?::Selecting a suitable and researchable topic.||Why is it important to keep accurate records during a research project?::Accurate records ensure reliable results and a valid conclusion can be drawn from the investigation.||Give an example of a simple biology research project topic.::The effect of different types of manure (or fertilizer) on the growth of maize seedlings.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe reproduction in plants (concept of reproduction in plants, asexual and sexual reproduction, pollination and fertilization)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction in plants and describe the processes of pollination and fertilization.
sla_teaching_aids: Hibiscus flowers|Bean flowers|Hand lens|Charts of flower structure
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Reproduction in plants is the process by which plants produce new individuals, and it may occur either asexually, without the fusion of sex cells, or sexually, through the fusion of male and female gametes.
sla_notes_details: Asexual reproduction in plants occurs through structures such as runners, tubers, bulbs and rhizomes, producing offspring genetically identical to the parent, while sexual reproduction involves the production of flowers containing male parts (stamens, producing pollen) and female parts (carpels, containing ovules). Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower, which may occur through agents such as insects, wind or water, and can be self-pollination, within the same flower or plant, or cross-pollination, between different plants. Fertilization follows pollination, where the pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovule, allowing the male nucleus to fuse with the female nucleus (egg cell) to form a zygote, which develops into a seed.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a hibiscus flower, insects such as bees are attracted by its bright petals and nectar, and as they move between flowers collecting nectar, pollen grains stick to their bodies and are transferred to the stigma of another flower, achieving cross-pollination.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding pollination helps farmers to encourage bees and other pollinators in their farms to improve fruit and seed production of crops.
sla_exercise: What is pollination?::The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.||State one difference between self-pollination and cross-pollination.::Self-pollination occurs within the same flower or plant, while cross-pollination occurs between flowers of different plants.||What is formed when the male and female nuclei fuse during fertilization in plants?::A zygote.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe reproduction in humans (sexual reproduction in human, fertilization, pregnancy and child birth)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the human reproductive systems and explain the processes of fertilization, pregnancy and child birth.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of male and female reproductive systems|Charts of stages of pregnancy|Family planning method charts
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Human reproduction is a sexual process involving the fusion of a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg/ovum) to form a new individual, followed by development inside the mother during pregnancy.
sla_notes_details: The male reproductive system produces sperm in the testes, while the female reproductive system produces eggs in the ovaries, one of which is usually released each month during ovulation. Fertilization occurs when a sperm cell fuses with an egg cell, usually in the oviduct (fallopian tube), forming a zygote that implants in the lining of the uterus and develops into an embryo and later a fetus during pregnancy, which lasts about nine months (40 weeks). During child birth, strong contractions of the uterus push the fully developed baby through the birth canal (vagina) to the outside world.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after fertilization in the oviduct, the zygote divides repeatedly as it moves down to the uterus, where it implants in the uterine wall about six to seven days after fertilization and begins to form the placenta, which supplies the developing fetus with nutrients and oxygen from the mother's blood.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding human reproduction is important for family planning, antenatal care and prevention of teenage pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.
sla_exercise: Where does fertilization normally take place in the human female?::In the oviduct (fallopian tube).||What structure supplies the developing fetus with nutrients and oxygen from the mother?::The placenta.||Approximately how long does human pregnancy last?::About nine months (approximately 40 weeks).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Describe the mechanisms of growth in mammals and flowering plants (concept of growth, mitosis and growth, growth and developmental stages in human and seed germination)
sla_name: Growth in Mammals and Flowering Plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the role of mitosis in growth and explain the developmental stages of humans and the process of seed germination.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of mitosis stages|Growth curve charts|Germinating seeds|Charts of human developmental stages
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Growth is a permanent increase in size, mass or number of cells of an organism, and in both mammals and flowering plants it occurs mainly through the cell division process called mitosis.
sla_notes_details: Mitosis is a type of cell division in which one cell divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells, allowing growth, replacement of worn-out cells and repair of damaged tissue. In humans, growth and development pass through stages such as infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood, each characterised by different rates and patterns of physical and physiological change. In flowering plants, growth begins with seed germination, the process by which a seed absorbs water, activates enzymes, and develops into a seedling, which may occur as epigeal germination, where the cotyledons are pushed above the soil, or hypogeal germination, where the cotyledons remain below the soil.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a germinating bean seed (epigeal germination), the hypocotyl elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the soil surface, whereas in a germinating maize seed (hypogeal germination), only the plumule emerges above the soil while the cotyledon remains underground.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding growth helps parents monitor their children's growth milestones, and helps farmers know the right planting depth and conditions for successful seed germination.
sla_exercise: What is mitosis?::A type of cell division in which one cell divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells.||Name the four main stages of human growth and development.::Infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood.||Distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination.::In epigeal germination the cotyledons are pushed above the soil, while in hypogeal germination the cotyledons remain below the soil.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the concepts, principles and processes of Biology
specific_competence_name: Describe the physiological, anatomical and ecological processes of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Explore the basic tenets of genetics (genetic materials, principles of inheritance, monohybrid, Mendelian and non-Mendelian inheritance; variation)
sla_name: Basic Principles of Genetics and Variation
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain the basic principles of inheritance and solve simple monohybrid genetic crosses.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts of DNA and chromosomes|Punnett square charts|Charts of Mendel's experiments
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Genetics is the branch of biology that studies heredity, the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring, through genetic material called DNA, which is organised into structures called chromosomes and genes.
sla_notes_details: Gregor Mendel's principles of inheritance describe how characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through pairs of factors, now known as alleles, one inherited from each parent; a monohybrid cross studies the inheritance of a single characteristic, such as flower colour, and can be represented using a Punnett square to predict the ratio of offspring with dominant and recessive traits. While many traits follow simple Mendelian dominant/recessive inheritance, some traits show non-Mendelian patterns, such as incomplete dominance, where the offspring show a blended trait, or codominance, where both alleles are equally expressed. Variation is the difference in characteristics among individuals of the same species, and it may be inherited (genetic) or caused by the environment, contributing to diversity within a population.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a monohybrid cross between a pea plant with the dominant allele for tall stems (T) and one with the recessive allele for short stems (t), a Punnett square of two heterozygous (Tt) parents predicts offspring in a ratio of 3 tall to 1 short.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding genetics helps in animal and crop breeding to select for desirable traits, and in understanding the inheritance of certain human traits and genetic conditions.
sla_exercise: What is an allele?::An alternative form of a gene that controls a particular characteristic.||In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Tt x Tt), what is the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring?::3 dominant (tall) to 1 recessive (short).||What is variation?::The difference in characteristics among individuals of the same species, which may be genetic or environmental in origin.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Carry out investigation related to reproduction in flowering plants (flower structure and embryo)
sla_name: Investigating Flower Structure and the Embryo
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly dissect a flower and identify its reproductive parts, and locate the embryo within a seed.
sla_teaching_aids: Hibiscus flowers|Razor blades|Forceps|Hand lens|Soaked bean seeds
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigating the structure of a flower and the embryo helps learners to directly observe the reproductive parts of a plant responsible for producing seeds.
sla_notes_details: To investigate flower structure, a flower such as a hibiscus is carefully dissected using a razor blade and forceps to separate and identify its parts: the sepals, petals, stamens (anther and filament) and carpel (stigma, style and ovary containing ovules). To locate the embryo, a soaked bean seed is cut open longitudinally to reveal the seed coat, cotyledons and the embryo, which consists of the plumule (young shoot) and radicle (young root).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when a soaked bean seed is split open, the tiny embryo can be seen attached between the two large cotyledons, with the plumule pointing towards one end and the radicle towards the other.
sla_notes_daily_life: This investigation helps farmers and gardeners understand seed structure when selecting healthy seeds for planting to ensure good germination.
sla_exercise: Name the male reproductive part of a flower.::The stamen (consisting of the anther and filament).||What two structures make up the embryo of a seed?::The plumule and the radicle.||Which flower part develops into the seed after fertilization?::The ovule.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills for conducting biological investigations
learning_activity_name: Investigate growth in flowering plants (hypogeal and epigeal germination)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly set up a germination experiment and distinguish between hypogeal and epigeal germination patterns.
sla_teaching_aids: Bean seeds|Maize seeds|Pots and soil|Water|Ruler
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigating germination allows learners to observe directly how different types of seeds germinate and grow, distinguishing between epigeal and hypogeal patterns.
sla_notes_details: In this investigation, bean seeds and maize seeds are planted separately in pots of moist soil and observed daily over one to two weeks. Bean seeds show epigeal germination, where the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above the soil surface where they turn green and may briefly perform photosynthesis, while maize seeds show hypogeal germination, where the cotyledon remains below the soil and only the plumule (young shoot) grows upward through the soil.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after one week, the bean seedlings show their two cotyledons visible above the soil, while the maize seedlings show only a single upright shoot with no cotyledons visible above ground.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these germination patterns helps farmers determine appropriate planting depths for different crops to ensure successful establishment.
sla_exercise: Which type of germination does a bean seed show?::Epigeal germination.||In hypogeal germination, does the cotyledon appear above or below the soil?::Below the soil.||Name one seed that shows hypogeal germination.::Maize.

specific_competence_name: Carry out a biological project work using biological principles
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit a report for the research project started in Form Three
sla_name: Completing and Submitting the Biology Research Project Report
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly complete their research project report with results, discussion and conclusion, and submit it within the required time.
sla_teaching_aids: Collected project data|Standard project report format|Computer/notebook for report writing
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Completing the biology research project involves finalising the investigation started in Form Three, analysing the collected data, and writing a complete report of the findings.
sla_notes_details: To complete the project, students first finish collecting any remaining data, then organise and analyse their results, often using tables, graphs or charts to summarise findings clearly. The final report should include an introduction/aim, background information, materials and methods, results, discussion of findings in relation to the aim, conclusion and recommendations, and should be submitted by the required deadline following the required format.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group that investigated the effect of manure on maize growth would present a graph showing the average height of maize plants under different manure treatments over several weeks, and conclude which treatment produced the best growth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Completing a research project develops important life skills such as planning, data analysis, scientific writing and meeting deadlines, all of which are valuable in further education and employment.
sla_exercise: What should be included in the discussion section of a project report?::An explanation of the results and how they relate to the aim of the investigation.||Why is it important to submit the project report by the required deadline?::Timely submission ensures the project is properly assessed and reflects good work planning and discipline.||Name one way results can be summarised clearly in a research report.::Using tables or graphs (charts) to present the data.
